title: Curriculum Has a Current
author: Meyer, Dan
summary: Observing three sixth-grade teachers teach the same Amplify Desmos Math lesson on number ordering, Dan Meyer develops the metaphor of curriculum having a 'current' -- an embedded set of pedagogical convictions about how learning ought to work -- and argues that teaching goes better when teachers swim with that current rather than against it. The specific lesson observed used a social, movement-based activity (students with number cards negotiating who is greater or lesser and arranging themselves in a line) which Meyer contrasts with a hypothetical worksheet covering the same math faster but missing the peer-negotiation and correction that deepen understanding. The three teachers he observed each found effective ways to channel the curriculum's conviction that 'students should become the curriculum': one drawing out class ideas to unconfuse himself, one playing with a student number card, one staying with a student's imprecise but correct utterance. Meyer's practical advice for teachers new to any curriculum is to sensitize themselves to the moments when a student's idea stretches the boundaries of the lesson -- to stay present, express genuine curiosity, and ask a second student to restate the idea, even just to buy thinking time. The article closes with a personal account of his months-long struggle as a tutor in a Spanish-speaking eighth-grade class, where earning enough trust to actually help took the entire school year -- an implicit challenge to AI tutoring enthusiasts to explain how a machine replicates that relational arc.
points: Curriculum embeds a 'current' -- a set of opinionated pedagogical convictions -- and teachers who understand and swim with it go faster and farther than those who swim across or against it; the first task with any new curriculum is to identify what it believes.

Social, movement-based number activities produce richer learning than equivalent worksheets because classmates negotiate and check each other's thinking in real time, and students are moving and talking rather than suffering through passive seat time.

The Amplify Desmos conviction that 'students should become the curriculum' means a student's imprecise-but-correct idea is a teaching moment to slow down and study, not correct and move past -- staying with it even briefly builds mathematical culture.

New teachers should sensitize themselves to the moments when student ideas stretch the lesson's boundaries: express surprise or interest, ask a second student to restate, and buy time to think -- you do not need to stay in that moment forever, just long enough to signal that student thinking is curriculum.

The relational work of tutoring -- months of pushing, prodding, and encouragement before earning enough trust to actually help with math -- is precisely what AI tutoring enthusiasts should be challenged to explain how a machine replicates.
quotes: Every curriculum -- every product and tool teachers use -- has a current, an expression of how its creators think things are and ought to be. Sometimes that current moves quickly, reflecting very opinionated creators. Other times, when its creators are more agnostic, the current moves slowly.

The paper can't check you like your classmates can. Every new conversation about numbers is an opportunity to negotiate your ideas with others. Over time, you're likely to find a person who disagrees with you. That's a valuable check for understanding.

Negotiating your ideas deepens your understanding. The student who can rip through the worksheet should have to explain why 9.6 is greater than 9.45 and in doing so strengthening their own understanding.

The third teacher heard an idea from a student, one that was correct but imprecisely expressed, and stuck with it, studying the kid as the kid said, 'So when the number gets bigger but the sign is negative the number is actually smaller.'

Sensitize yourself to the moments when students reveal their curriculum. A kid will say something that might seem out of bounds at first but which is actually working to stretch the boundaries of what we call math. In those moments, stay present.

Ask a second kid to restate the first kid's thought even if just to buy yourself time to think. Ask the class to use their hands to signal whether they agree or have questions. You do not need to stay in this moment forever -- just long enough to convince one more kid that they too might be the curriculum.

Last week, the kid who kind of runs the group asked me what my name was. 'What do I call you if I want your help?' he said. 'Mr. Dan,' I said. There are four weeks left in the school year and I finally have -- for now! tentatively! -- enough trust and goodwill to help them with math.
